extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students studying proof techniques / readers of a solutions appendix
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and worked examples for proving/disproving quantified statements, limits, sequences, induction proofs, and related elementary analysis/number-theory arguments found in a textbook solutions appendix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation of quantified statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Write out the negation of a quantified statement explicitly (swap ∀ and ∃ and negate the predicate) before attempting disproof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples on the page: negation of ∀x ∈ P, ∀y ∈ P, x + y ∈ P becomes ∃x ∈ P s.t. ∃y ∈ P s.t. x + y ∉ P; negation forms are used repeatedly to reduce a proof-of-falsity to finding witnesses/counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disprove universal statements by counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a universal statement false, exhibit a concrete element (or elements) that violate it (a counterexample).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to disprove 'for all primes x,y, x+y is prime', pick x=y=3 giving x+y=6 ∉ P. Page repeatedly uses this pattern: write negation (existence of a counterexample) and provide explicit witness(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove existential statements by providing a witness
rubrics_metrics.description: When the statement is existential (∃), prove it by constructing a particular example (a witness) satisfying the required property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to prove ∃a∈A, ∃b∈B such that a+b∈C, take a=0, b=1. The solutions emphasize 'since both quantifiers are there exists, we only need an example'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of case analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Split the argument into cases that exhaust possibilities (e.g., parity, x=2 vs x odd) and handle each separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: handle primes by cases 'x=2 or x odd'; handle y even/odd separately when showing x=7 works for all y; proofs and disproofs frequently proceed by case-splitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication truth when hypothesis false
rubrics_metrics.description: An implication P ⇒ Q is automatically true when the hypothesis P is false; exploit this in proof by choosing values making the hypothesis false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly: pick x=0 or y=0 to make xy>0 false, thus implication holds trivially. The page explicitly notes 'when the hypothesis is false, the implication is always true.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive proofs for ∀∃ statements
rubrics_metrics.description: For statements of the form ∀x ∃y such that ..., give a rule/construction for y in terms of x (explicit formula or selection) and prove it works for arbitrary x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to show ∀z ∈ R, ∃x with x+y=z pick x=z−y; many solutions use this constructive method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using known properties (parity, unique even prime)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage simple arithmetic facts (e.g., 2 is the only even prime, parity of sums/products) to simplify arguments and produce witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sum of two odd primes is even and >2 hence not prime; use parity to choose y=x so x+y even and not prime; these facts serve as shortcuts in disproofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by counterexample for existential negations
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a universal negation (i.e., original existential is false), exhibit for each relevant case a choice that forces the predicate to fail, often by giving a method to pick b ∈ B depending on a ∈ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: To negate '∃a∈A s.t. ∀b∈B a+b∈C' show ∀a ∃b a+b∉C by, for each a, choosing b=6 or 3 as appropriate so 6|(a+b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Epsilon-delta proofs (limits of functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given ε>0, choose δ (often as a simple function of ε) and bound |f(x) - L| by an expression involving |x - a| to make it < ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: take δ=ε/3 for linear functions; take δ=min{1,ε/3} for quadratic-related estimates; use elementary inequalities and algebraic manipulation to obtain the required bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence convergence via N(ε) argument
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove sequence convergence, for given ε>0 choose N (often dependent on ε) so that for n≥N the tail terms satisfy desired inequality |s_n-L|<ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: pick N = ceil(M^2)+1 for sequences involving 1/√n or choose N based on bounds 5/n2 < ε in proofs; use comparisons 1/n3 ≤ 1/n2 etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving divergence / failure of convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: Show divergence by finding an ε>0 such that for every N there exists n≥N with |s_n-L|≥ε (produce explicit subsequence or alternating examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: alternating sequences (−1)^n + 1/n fail to converge to 0; choose ε like 1/2 and show no N works because subsequence values remain at distance ≥1/2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounding techniques using simple inequalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use elementary bounds (like |sin θ| ≤ 1 or |x+1| ≤ 3 when |x−1|≤1) to reduce complex expressions to multiples of |x−a| or other controlled quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to show 6x sin(1/x)→0 use |sin(·)| ≤ 1 so |f(x)| ≤ 6|x| and choose δ accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequences: convergence implies boundedness
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sequence converges to L then it is bounded; construct the bound using finitely many leading terms and the limit neighborhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page gives method: find N with |a_n−L|<1 for n≥N, then take M = max{|a_1|,...,|a_{N−1}|, |L|+1}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone sequences and +∞ behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: For increasing sequences, either they are bounded (hence converge) or they diverge to +∞; to show not +∞ produce a uniform upper bound or show existence of small values preventing +∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: construct C so that some m≥n has a_m < C and use monotonicity to bound earlier terms; converses are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifying metric properties by exhaustive casework
rubrics_metrics.description: For piecewise-defined distances, demonstrate triangle inequality and other metric axioms by splitting into cases (equality/inequality of points) and checking subcases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for D(x,y)=0 if x=y else 1, check cases x=z, x≠z and subcases x=y or x≠y to show D(x,z) ≤ D(x,y)+D(y,z).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical induction (standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use base case and inductive step: assume statement for n=k, then prove for n=k+1; this structure is used across many algebraic and combinatorial identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple worked examples: divisibility proofs, inequalities, factorial and power comparisons, sum formulas. The page emphasises verifying base case(s) and algebraic manipulations in inductive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong induction
rubrics_metrics.description: When the step for n+1 depends on several previous cases, assume the statement holds for all smaller indices up to k and use that to prove k+1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Fibonacci divisibility proof uses strong induction to show F_q | F_{qn} for all n by representing F_{n+ℓ} in terms of previous Fibonacci numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive multiplication of solutions for existential equations
rubrics_metrics.description: To extend existential solutions (e.g., existence of integer solutions x^2+y^2=z^{2k+1}) use algebraic operations to produce new solutions from existing ones (e.g., scale by z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: given x^2+y^2=z^{2k+1}, multiply both sides by z^2 to get (xz)^2+(yz)^2=z^{2(k+1)+1} and note xz,yz,z≥2 preserve conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using algebraic identities in induction (reindexing, Pascal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reindex sums and apply combinatorial identities (Pascal's identity) to manipulate binomial/sum formulas in inductive proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Binomial Theorem proof uses reindexing and Pascal's identity; summation identities use factoring and algebraic rearrangement to show closed forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher-order derivative formulas via induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove general formulas for k-th derivatives of simple power or power-like functions by induction using the basic derivative rules (power rule, chain rule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: derivative of x^n gives n!/(n−k)! x^{n−k} formula; prove base case then differentiate the k-th derivative to get (k+1)-th derivative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplace transform of derivatives by induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use integration by parts and decay assumptions at infinity to derive ℒ{f^{(k)}}(s) = s^k ℒ{f}(s) − sum_{i=0}^{k−1} s^{k−1−i} f^{(i)}(0) via induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base case k=1 via integration by parts; then assume formula for k and apply integration by parts again to get k+1, using hypotheses that boundary terms vanish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of calculus techniques (l'Hôpital, integration by parts) with induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine analysis tools with inductive reasoning to evaluate limits/integrals involving polynomial-exponential forms and factorials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: proving lim_{x→∞} x^n e^{−x}=0 by induction using l'Hôpital; evaluating ∫_0^∞ x^n e^{−x} dx = n! by integration by parts and induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof strategy remark: iterate and refine proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: It's normal to produce a more complicated proof first and then 'better' proofs later; multiple approaches can be valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explicitly notes that early proofs are often improved by later ones; encourages trying different methods (cases, induction, direct algebra).
